3 The algorithm
[id=S3.p1.1] Our algorithm, PEPO, applies three important changes on top of DPO, which will enable our guarantees featuring only the single-policy concentrability coefficient: (1) We derive a pessimistic DPO objective ℒpessDPO\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pessDPO}} derived from a Bradley-Terry model variant which allows ties.
(2) We split the dataset into LL subsets of equal size and we maximize LL different instances of the pessimistic DPO objective with respect to independent LoRA parameters over each subset.
(3) Finally, our theory motivates outputting a policy obtained by aggregating the ensemble in a pessimistic manner. Unfortunately, computing this policy is intractable, but we present a rejection sampling method to sample exactly from it.
[id=S3.p2.1] We now move to a detailed overview of these three components, whose interplay is key for the theoretical guarantees presented in the next section.
[id=S3.SS1]
3.1 Bradley-Terry model with ties
[id=S3.SS1.p1.1] In our analysis presented in Section 4, we need to build a pessimistic estimator for the winning probabilities probability under the ground truth Bradley-Terry model, i.e., we look for ℙ^:𝒳×𝒜×𝒜∈[0,1]\hat{\mathbb{P}}:\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\in[0,1] such that for all a,b∈𝒜×𝒜a,b\in{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{A}} and x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, we have that ℙ^​(a≻b|x)≤ℙr⋆true​(a≻b|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(a\succ b|x)\leq\mathbb{P}^{\mathrm{true}}_{r^{\star}}(a\succ b|x).
[id=S3.SS1.p2.1] Clearly, ℙ^\hat{\mathbb{P}} cannot be a proper estimator, i.e., it cannot be a sigmoid function. Indeed, let us assume that for some reward rr, we choose ℙ^​(a≻b|x)=σ⁡(Δr​(x,a,b))\hat{\mathbb{P}}(a\succ b|x)=\sigma(\Delta_{r}(x,a,b)). Then, if Δr​(x,a,b)≤Δr⋆​(x,a,b)\Delta_{r}(x,a,b)\leq\Delta_{r^{\star}}(x,a,b), we have that by the monotonicity of σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot), it holds that ℙ^​(a≻b|x)≤ℙr⋆true​(a≻b|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(a\succ b|x)\leq\mathbb{P}^{\mathrm{true}}_{r^{\star}}(a\succ b|x), satisfying the requirement for this ordering of aa and bb.
[id=S3.SS1.p3.1] However, when the two actions are exchanged, recall that by definition Δr​(x,a,b)=−Δr​(x,b,a)\Delta_{r}(x,a,b)=-\Delta_{r}(x,b,a) and Δr⋆​(x,a,b)=−Δr⋆​(x,b,a)\Delta_{r^{\star}}(x,a,b)=-\Delta_{r^{\star}}(x,b,a).
Moreover, since σ⁡(x)=1−σ⁡(−x)\sigma(x)=1-\sigma(-x), ℙ^​(a≻b|x)≤ℙr⋆true​(a≻b|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(a\succ b|x)\leq\mathbb{P}^{\mathrm{true}}_{r^{\star}}(a\succ b|x) unfortunately implies that ℙ^​(b≻a|x)≥ℙr⋆true​(b≻a|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(b\succ a|x)\geq\mathbb{P}^{\mathrm{true}}_{r^{\star}}(b\succ a|x). Therefore, for proper estimators, underestimating the winning probability of action aa against bb implies overestimating the win rate of bb against aa, whereby failing to underestimate both winning probabilities.
[id=S3.SS1.p4.1] To overcome the issue, we need to look at improper estimators. In particular, we need to estimate ℙ^\hat{\mathbb{P}} within a class of models which does not force ℙ^​(b≻a|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(b\succ a|x) and ℙ^​(a≻b|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(a\succ b|x)
to sum up to 11. Our idea is, therefore, to predict ℙ^\hat{\mathbb{P}} within the class of Bradley-Terry models with ties introduced in the sequel. Having a third event in the distribution’s support allows now the sum of ℙ^​(b≻a|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(b\succ a|x) and ℙ^​(a≻b|x)\hat{\mathbb{P}}(a\succ b|x) to be equal to some value c≤1c\leq 1. Then the comparison between aa and bb is declared a tie with probability 1−c1-c. We formally introduce the Bradley-Terry models with ties below.
Definition 3.1.
[id=S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1] Bradley-Terry model with ties
The Bradley-Terry preference model with ties, associated to a reward function rr, computes the probability of aa being a winner over bb in response to the prompt xx as
[id=S3.Ex3]
ℙr​(a≻b|x)=exp⁡(β​Δr​(x,a,b)/2)Z⁡(x,a,b),\mathbb{P}_{r}(a\succ b|x)=\frac{\exp\left({\beta\Delta_{r}(x,a,b)/2}\right)}{Z(x,a,b)},
[id=S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2] where given a tie weight λ:𝒳×𝒜×𝒜→[0,∞)\lambda:\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow[0,\infty) which satisfies λ⁡(x,a,b)=λ⁡(x,b,a)\lambda(x,a,b)=\lambda(x,b,a), we defined
[id=S3.Ex4]
Z⁡(x,a,b):=exp⁡(β​Δr​(x,a,b)/2)+exp⁡(β​Δr​(x,b,a)/2)+λ⁡(x,a,b).Z(x,a,b):=\exp\left({\beta\Delta_{r}(x,a,b)/2}\right)+\exp\left({\beta\Delta_{r}(x,b,a)/2}\right)+\lambda(x,a,b).
[id=S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.3] Moreover, the comparison is declared a tie with probability
𝔭tie​(x,a,b)=λ⁡(x,a,b)Z⁡(x,a,b)\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}(x,a,b)=\frac{\lambda(x,a,b)}{Z(x,a,b)}.
[id=S3.SS1.p5.1] While modification of the Bradley-Terry models to allow ties already appeared in classical statistics (Rao and Kupper, 1967; Davidson, 1970) and have been used recently in the RLHF/DPO literature (Chen et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a), we did not find the model described above to already exist in the exact same form. In particular, it is important for our theoretical analysis that the tie probability weight λ\lambda can depend on the triplet x,a,bx,a,b involved in the comparison, while in (Rao and Kupper, 1967; Davidson, 1970) the ties probability weights are prompt and answers independent. Moreover, notice that λ⁡(x,a,b)=0\lambda(x,a,b)=0 for all x,a,bx,a,b recovers the standard BT model.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1]
Pessimistic interpretation of shifted sigmoid functions
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] An important observation about Definition 3.1 is that we can rewrite ℙr​(a≻b|x)\mathbb{P}_{r}(a\succ b|x) as
[id=S3.EGx1]
σ⁡(β​Δr​(x,a,b)−log⁡(1+λ⁡(x,a,b)​eβ​Δr​(x,a,b)/2)⏟Shift)=σpess​(β​Δr​(x,a,b),λ⁡(x,a,b)),\displaystyle\sigma(\beta\Delta_{r}(x,a,b)-\underbrace{\log(1+\lambda(x,a,b)e^{\beta\Delta_{r}(x,a,b)/2})}_{\mathrm{Shift}})=\sigma_{\mathrm{pess}}(\beta\Delta_{r}(x,a,b),\lambda(x,a,b)),
(5)
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] where we define the pessimistic sigmoid function as σpess​(x,λ):=σ⁡(x−log⁡(1+λ​ex/2))\sigma_{\mathrm{pess}}(x,\lambda):=\sigma(x-\log(1+\lambda e^{x/2})). Notice that σpess\sigma_{\mathrm{pess}} is a sigmoid function translated on the right.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] This observation surprisingly allows us to connect our pessimistic technique to the extensive literature on DPO with margins. Indeed, we highlight in passing that right-shifted sigmoid functions have already been used in literature with the motivation of ensuring a margin, at least as large as Shift\mathrm{Shift}, between the winner and the loser response (Touvron et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024). On the opposite side, (Gupta et al., 2024) shifts the sigmoid on the left which can be interpreted as an optimistic exploration strategy that becomes useful when the Bradley Terry model can be queried online and not exclusively on an offline dataset. We offer an additional discussion on this point in Appendix B and we now move to the second important component of our algorithm.

3.2 Creating the models ensemble
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] We build on the pessimistic sigmoid function to train LL pessimistic language models over a partition of the preference dataset. To this end, we partition the data 𝒟={Xn,An+,An−}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\left\{{X_{n},A^{+}_{n},A^{-}_{n}}\right\}^{N}_{n=1} in LL subsets, i.e., 𝒟=∪Lℓ=1𝒟ℓ\mathcal{D}=\cup^{L}_{\ell=1}\mathcal{D}^{\ell},
where we denote the data in the ℓth\ell^{\mathrm{th}} chunk as 𝒟ℓ={Xn,ℓ,An,ℓ+,An,ℓ−}\mathcal{D}^{\ell}=\left\{{X_{n,\ell},A^{+}_{n,\ell},A^{-}_{n,\ell}}\right\} .
At this point, we compute π~ℓ\tilde{\pi}^{\ell} for each ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L] as the solution of the following pessimistic DPO objective which modifies the original DPO objective in (4) by using only the subset 𝒟ℓ\mathcal{D}^{\ell} instead of using the full dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} and replacing the standard sigmoid with σpess\sigma_{\mathrm{pess}} in (5):
[id=S3.EGx2]
π~ℓ\displaystyle\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}

In our analysis, 𝔭tieℓ​(x,a,b)\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}^{\ell}(x,a,b) should be set closer to 11, whenever the triplet x,a,bx,a,b feels very uncertain for the model π~ℓ\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}. Having a dependence on the ensemble index thus allows us to instantiate models with different levels of confidence for different regions of the state action space.
Moreover, we maximize (6) over a subset of Π\Pi denoted by Π¯\bar{\Pi}, defined as Π¯:={π∈Π:|β​Δlog⁡π/πref|≤2​Rmax}\bar{\Pi}:=\left\{{\pi\in\Pi:\left|{\beta\Delta_{\log\pi/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}\right|\leq 2R_{\max}}\right\}. [id=S3.SS3.p1.1] We now aim at aggregating the LL models in the ensemble in a pessimistic manner. [id=S3.SS4.p1.1] The structure of our efficient sampling scheme leverages the closed form solution of (7) which is offered by the following lemma.
Lemma 3.2.
[id=S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1] The policy πout\pi_{\mathrm{out}} defined as solution of the optimization problem in (7) satisfies for all x,a∈𝒳×𝒜x,a\in\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}
[id=S3.Ex9]
πout​(a|x)=minℓ∈[L]⁡π~ℓ​(a|x)​exp⁡(−B​𝔭tie¯​(x,a)/β)∑a∈𝒜minℓ∈[L]⁡π~ℓ​(a|x)​exp⁡(−B​𝔭tie¯​(x,a)/β).\pi_{\mathrm{out}}(a|x)=\frac{\min_{\ell\in[L]}\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(a|x)\exp\left({\nicefrac{{-B\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}}(x,a)}}{{\beta}}}\right)}{\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}\min_{\ell\in[L]}\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(a|x)\exp\left({\nicefrac{{-B\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}}(x,a)}}{{\beta}}}\right)}.
[id=S3.SS4.p2.1] For the following discussion, let us denote the numerator of πout\pi_{\mathrm{out}} as
[id=S3.Ex10]
fout​(x,a):=minℓ∈[L]⁡π~ℓ​(a|x)​exp⁡(−B​𝔭tie¯​(x,a)/β),f_{\mathrm{out}}(x,a):=\min_{\ell\in[L]}\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(a|x)\exp\left({\nicefrac{{-B\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}}(x,a)}}{{\beta}}}\right),

Therefore, the computation of the denominator which involves a sum over the response space 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is not tractable. However, rejection sampling (see Algorithm 2) is a very attractive solution in our scenario. Indeed, any model in the ensemble can serve as an ideal proposal distribution since they upper bound fout​(x,a)f_{\mathrm{out}}(x,a) everywhere. To see this, notice that B​𝔭tie¯≥0B\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}}\geq 0 and that minℓ∈[L]⁡π~ℓ​(a|x)≤π~ℓ′​(a|x)\min_{\ell\in[L]}\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(a|x)\leq\tilde{\pi}^{\ell^{\prime}}(a|x) for any ℓ′\ell^{\prime}. These facts ensure that for any model π~ℓ\tilde{\pi}^{\ell} the ratio fout​(x,a)/π~ℓ​(a|x)≤1f_{\mathrm{out}}(x,a)/\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(a|x)\leq 1 for all x,a∈𝒳×𝒜x,a\in\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}.

[id=S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1]
Discussion of the hyperparameter
[id=S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] In our practical implementation 𝔭tie¯,λℓ\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}},\lambda^{\ell} and LL are treated as hyperparameters. Moreover, while 𝔭tie¯\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}} needs to be state-action dependent for our analysis, we consider it as constant in practice. Despite this simplification, we still observe improvements over the baselines we consider. In practice, we did not observe the practical performance to be significantly impacted by the choices for 𝔭tie¯\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}} and λℓ\lambda^{\ell}, at least in the ablation range we considered. LL is a more important hyperparameter as shown by our ablation presented in Appendix A.
[id=S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] Finally, we provide our algorithm pseudocode in Algorithm 1 and we move to the theoretical analysis of PEPO.

[id=S4.SS1]
4.1 Analysis sketch
[id=S4.SS1.p1.1] For clarity, we still operate under the benign assumption that ∑bπdata​(b|x)​r⋆​(x,b)=∑bπdata​(b|x)​log⁡π~ℓ​(b|x)πref​(b|x)\sum_{b}\pi_{\mathrm{data}}(b|x)r^{\star}(x,b)=\sum_{b}\pi_{\mathrm{data}}(b|x)\log\frac{\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(b|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(b|x)} but we clarify how this assumption can be removed in Appendix E.1. The analysis has three main conceptual steps.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1]
Step 1: Establishing pessimism
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] A fundamental quantity of the analysis is the implicitly estimated reward gap Δ^​(x,a,b)\widehat{\Delta}(x,a,b), defined as
[id=S4.EGx3]
Δ^​(x,a,b):=β⁡(minℓ∈[L]⁡log⁡π~ℓ​(a|x)πref​(a|x)−maxℓ∈[L]⁡log⁡π~ℓ​(b|x)πref​(b|x))−B​𝔭tie¯​(x,a)\displaystyle\widehat{\Delta}(x,a,b):=\beta\left({\min_{\ell\in[L]}\log\frac{\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(a|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a|x)}-\max_{\ell\in[L]}\log\frac{\tilde{\pi}^{\ell}(b|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(b|x)}}\right)-B\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}}(x,a)
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] which with high probability is a lower bound on the average reward gap under r⋆r^{\star} when the second action is sampled from πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}}.

On the optimal ensemble size
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] Our analysis provides precise guidelines for choosing LL. In particular, Lemma 4.4 shows that the generalization error increases with LL. Therefore, we would like to choose it as small as possible. However, Lemma 4.2 imposes a lower bound on LL for the pessimism to hold. Hence, the conclusion that LL should be the smallest value which ensures that the estimator Δ^\widehat{\Delta} is pessimistic with high enough probability.

A.1 Ablation for the ensemble size LL in a controlled setting.
[id=A1.SS1.p1.1] We run an ablation for the ensemble size LL in a simple and controlled setting. The environment under consideration, we consider an empty prompt set and 2020 possible answers. The preferences are generated via the Bradley-Terry model with rewards which are all gaussian distributed. In particular, all rewards distribution but the one of the optimal arm have mean equal to 11 and variance equal to 11. On the other hand, the optimal arm’s distribution has mean equal to 2.92.9 and variance equal to 1/21/2. We generate preference datasets of different sizes 𝒟\mathcal{D} and run PEPO for different ensemble sizes LL. We report the results in Figure 3 where we see that for all the values we tried PEPO finds the optimal action for all the 55 considered seeds. However, the strongest performance is obtained for L=3L=3. Increasing LL, above 33 slows down learning. This is consistent with the theoretical guideline of setting LL to smallest value which is large enough to ensure pessimism.

A.2 Details for the experiments in the controlled setting
[id=A1.SS2.p1.1] For , we used πdata=πref=[0.04,0.93,0.03]\pi_{\mathrm{data}}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=[0.04,0.93,0.03]. That is, the largest mass is on the central action, which is the optimal one. This makes the optimal action well-covered, i.e. small C⋆C^{\star}, therefore χ2\chi^{2}PO and PEPO can work reliably. At the same time, the all-policy concentrability is large because the two suboptimal actions are poorly covered. This explains why DPO is outperformed in .
For the unknown case, we consider instead πdata=[0.04,0.93,0.03]\pi_{\mathrm{data}}=[0.04,0.93,0.03] and πref=[0.00025,0.00025,0.9995]\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=[0.00025,0.00025,0.9995] and β=0.001\beta=0.001. In this case, we have two distinct failure modes for DPO and χ2\chi^{2}PO while PEPO still works reliably. DPO fails because the all-policy concentrability is still very large. This implies that the reward of the suboptimal actions can not be estimated accurately, and, therefore, there is the risk of playing a suboptimal action whose reward is wrongly overestimated. The failure mode of χ2\chi^{2}PO is instead different. The mismatch between πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}} and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} leads χ2\chi^{2}PO to perceive the suboptimal action with high probability under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} as accurately estimated. On the contrary, since the optimal action has low mass under πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, this action is perceived as quite uncertain. All in all, χ2\chi^{2}PO concludes that the high reward estimate for the optimal action can not be trusted and plays a suboptimal action. PEPO still succeeds in this setting because under πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}}, we have that the optimal action is actually estimated more accurately than the suboptimal ones. PEPO can use this fact to successfully identify and play the optimal action if the dataset size is large enough. This is shown in .
